section.title: About the formal grammars
section.para: formal grammarrole of Lojban was designed so that a formal definition could state its grammar, and the designers largely achieved that aim. A formal grammar is a precise definition that a machine can test. This chapter presents two of them. The first defines the word forms: which strings of letters are words in the first place, and where each word begins and ends (see ). The second defines the syntax: which strings of words are grammatical text, and what structure each such text has (see ).
The rules for the word-level magic words are in . Those rules, along with the unsettled corners this chapter notes below, lie outside what the printed grammars decide.

formal grammarstatus of versions EBNF grammarstatus of YACC grammarremoved from print, 2014 third baselineThe official grammar of Lojban syntax is the YACC grammar of the third baseline, which is the one the Logical Language Group adopted. The first edition of this book printed that grammar in full, alongside an EBNF form of the same grammar, and declared the YACC version authoritative should the two ever disagree. In 2014, however, an informal majority at the annual meeting of the LLG chose to print only the EBNF, in order to save pages. The YACC listing can still be found in the electronic supplements to this book, and the history of that decision is told in .

EBNF grammaras the grammar of this editionThe EBNF printed in this chapter is the grammar of the language that this book describes. It is the EBNF of the third baseline, with a small number of changes, each of which is marked where it is made and listed in . Some of the changes correct misprints of the first edition. Some state what this book teaches and the baseline grammar did not express, such as the committee's decision on tag binding. Wherever this grammar departs from the official grammar, the mark says so. A reader who wants the exact behavior of the official parser should consult the YACC grammar and the parser itself.

camxesas de facto compatibility target Meanwhile, the working grammars of the community use a different formal system: parsing expression grammars (PEG). These cover morphology and syntax together, and they include the amendments that the language-definition committee adopted, which this book describes throughout. The standard camxes PEG is the principal de facto target for compatibility across the tools this edition surveyed. Some of those tools implement it directly, and others reimplement its behavior. All of this is de facto, not official.

Of the camxes PEG, this chapter prints only the part that defines word forms (see ). That part is a precise, formal definition of how a stream of sounds breaks into words. For syntax we print the EBNF grammar instead, so the camxes PEG for syntax is not in this book.

Sometimes the text of this book disagrees with the amendments. When that happens, the amendments prevail, and the book flags each one where it teaches it. The EBNF below already includes the amendments that change syntax, with their marks.

tagsbinding to selbri, in the EBNF grammar tensesbefore forethought connectives, in the EBNF grammar The rules below stand in for the magic words (quotation, erasure, and their kin) with nothing but placeholders, since the real behavior of those words is a matter of the word level, and specifies it rule by rule. That chapter also covers the genuinely unsettled sa. How the words of a text become the input of the EBNF is explained in . Two further points that the first edition's grammar left open, namely the binding of a tag to a following selbri and a bare tense before a forethought connective, are settled in , each with its status.

section.title: PEG word-form grammar
section.para: PEG word-form grammarfull text of slinku'i testformal statement of This section reproduces the formal definition of Lojban word forms. It is the morphology part of the PEG that current Lojban software implements, and it states precisely what and present informally. These rules decide which strings of letters are cmevla, cmavo, and brivla, where words begin and end, and which letter sequences Lojban permits at all.

The grammar is the one the camxes parser family uses, at the revision this edition pinned for its verification work. It was written by Jorge Llambias (la .xorxes.). Every rule below appears exactly as his file defines it. The file itself, though, is a plain-text program, so this section lays it out for readers: each rule appears under its own name, and headings group the rules. The arrow between the name of a rule and its definition is ← here, where the file writes <-.

The file is under the MIT license.
prints its copyright and permission notices, which also cover the rules in this section.

Every rule definition appears with its own characters, in the order of the file. We changed, reordered, or omitted none of them; the typesetting changes only the material around them. The headings of the subsections come from this edition, not from the file (which had only three headings of its own). The implementation directives after a few rules are in italics. The comments of the file appear here as prose: we quote some, summarize others, and leave out one bibliographic link to the parsing literature.

PEG word-form grammarstatus of
This grammar is the de facto standard definition of Lojban word forms, and current software implements it. Within it, the ban on a consonant followed by a glide is separately committee-approved. For the full history of its authority, see .

A parsing expression grammar differs from the more familiar grammar notations in one important way: the choice operator / is ordered. When there are several alternatives, the parser takes the first one that succeeds and never tries the rest. The grammar also has two lookahead operators, & (the following material must be present) and ! (the following material must be absent). Ordered choice and lookahead together make the grammar deterministic, so it divides any stream of Lojban sounds into words in exactly one way.
Here is the full notation:

listitem.para: A rule has the form name ← expression, which means that the expression parses the construct called name.
Concatenation is juxtaposition: you write the parts next to each other, with no operator between them.
/ is ordered choice, as described above.
? makes the element to its left optional.
* lets the element to its left repeat zero or more times.
+ lets the element to its left repeat one or more times.
Both * and + take as many repetitions as they can.
& requires what follows it to be present, and ! requires it to be absent. Neither consumes any text.
. stands for any character, [] for a class of characters, and text in quotation marks for itself.
An italic note such as #: PUSH after a rule is a directive to the implementation, not a part of the rule. The ZOI rules explain the directives used here.

section.title: Words and ZOI quotes
section.para: The source file opens with three wrapper rules. It keeps them as comments, because they belong to the parser and not to the grammar proper. They say this:

listitem.para: A text is an optional pause followed by any number of words, each optionally followed by a pause.
A word is either a Lojban word or a non-Lojban word.
A Lojban word is a cmevla, a cmavo, or a brivla.

section.para: The two rules here state the last of these, and they attach the spaces that can follow a word.

The source file explains the problem in its own words: Pure PEG cannot handle ZOI quotes, because it cannot check whether the closing delimiter is the same as the opening one. ZOI quote handling is the only part of Lojban's grammar that needs mechanisms external to the pure PEG grammar to be implemented properly; those mechanisms are implementation-specific. So the four rules below carry implementation directives, shown in italics. Three of them handle the delimiters:

listitem.para: PEEK-DIFF requires the quoted text to differ from it.
POP-EQ requires the closing delimiter to equal it.

section.para: The fourth directive here is LEAF, on the rule zoi_word_2. LEAF also appears on one rule elsewhere in the grammar, and JOIN appears on three others. These two directives concern how an implementation builds its parse tree, and the source file does not define them.

section.title: About this grammar
section.para: This EBNF document is explicitly dedicated to the public domain by its author, The Logical Language Group, Inc. Contact that organization at: 2904 Beau Lane, Fairfax VA 22031 USA 703-385-0273 (intl: +1 703 385 0273)

EBNF grammarrelation to the official grammarThis section prints the EBNF grammar of the language that this book describes, which is the EBNF of the third baseline plus the changes listed in . Each change is marked where it is made, along with its status. The official grammar of Lojban syntax is the YACC grammar of the third baseline, as explains; wherever this grammar departs from it, the departure belongs to this edition, and the mark says so.
Explanation of notation: All rules have the form:
name number = bnf-expression

which means that the grammatical construct name is defined by bnf-expression. The number cross-references this grammar with the rule numbers in the YACC grammar. The names are the same as those in the YACC grammar, except that subrules are labeled with A, B, C, ... in the YACC grammar and with 1, 2, 3, ... in this grammar. In addition, rule 971 is simple_tag in the YACC grammar but stag in this grammar, because of its frequent appearance.

listitem.para: Names in lower case are grammatical constructs.
Names in UPPER CASE are selma'o (lexeme) names, and are terminals.
Concatenation is expressed by juxtaposition with no operator symbol.
& represents and/or. A & B is the same as A | B | A B but not B A. Furthermore, A & B & C & D permits one or more of A, B, C, and/or D, but only in that order.
... represents optional repetition of the construct to the left. Left-grouping is implied; right-grouping is shown by explicit self-referential recursion with no ...
() serves to indicate the grouping of the other operators. Otherwise, ... binds closer than &, which binds closer than |.
# is shorthand for [free ...] , a construct which appears in many places.
// encloses an elidable terminator, which may be omitted (without change of meaning) if no grammatical ambiguity results.
Juxtaposition binds closer than &, so A B & C D is (A B) & (C D). Any rule that needs the other reading uses parentheses.
x ... means one x, optionally followed by more. [x ...] and [x] ... both mean any number of x, including none.

/X#/ is an elidable terminator together with its free-modifier slot. When X is elided, the slot goes with it, so a free modifier cannot follow an elided X. /X/ # keeps the slot whether or not X is written.

section.para: Points 11 to 13 are additions of this edition. The first edition's notation never said how juxtaposition binds, and its point 6 read A & B as A | B | A B, without the restriction on order. That restriction and the three added points simply state how this grammar reads its own rules; they change no rule.

The terminals of the grammar are the selma'o of , together with two more classes: BRIVLA, which is the class of every gismu, lujvo and fu'ivla, and CMEVLA, which is the class of every name word. says how a text becomes the stream of such words that the rules read. The rules refer to each other by name, and lists, for each name, every rule that refers to it.

Because terminators can be elided, some texts fit the rules in more than one way. gives the rules by which this grammar chooses a single reading, and the prose of each subsection points there wherever a rule needs it.

section.title: The text and its paragraphs
section.para: A text is what one speaker or writer produces, from the first word to the last. A text can open with any of these forms:

listitem.para: nai, a vague negation at the start of a text (see ).
A run of names, which serves as a form of address without a vocative.
Indicators or free modifiers that belong to the whole text.
A connective, joik-jek, that joins this text to a previous one in afterthought (afterthought being the style in which a connective is placed between its operands).

section.para: After that come the paragraphs. Rule 2, text-1, permits initial .i sentence separators, then ni'o topic markers, or either of them alone. Each .i can carry an afterthought connective and a tense grouped with bo, and a speaker can use this to continue another speaker's text (see ). ni'o marks a change of topic, and repeated ni'o markers indicate larger breaks (see ). A paragraph, in turn, contains statements or fragments separated by .i.

EBNF grammarcorrections, text-1Rule 2 is corrected here. The first edition printed its two parts as alternatives, so that a text began either with .i forms or with ni'o markers, but not with both in that order. The YACC grammar, however, lets any number of .i forms precede a run of ni'o, and .i ni'o mi klama is a text. This edition prints that form.

section.title: Statements and fragments
section.para: A statement is a sentence, a sentence with a prenex before it, or several sentences joined by afterthought connectives (see ). A prenex is a clause prefix, terms zo'u, which binds variables or sets topics for the sentence that follows (see ). The grouping of the connectives is settled by the four levels of the statement rules.

Rule 11, statement, takes any number of prenexes. Rule 12, statement-1, joins statements with .i followed by a jek or a joik: .i je, .i ja nai, .i joi. These group to the left, by the left-grouping rule of logical connectives (see and ), so A .i je B .i ja C means (A and B) or C. The statement after each connective is optional, which is why a bare .i je can end a text.

Rule 13, statement-2, is the right-grouping form. An .i with an optional connective and an optional tense, followed by bo, binds the sentence after it more tightly than a plain .i je does. The rule refers to itself on its right, and so a series of .i bo connections groups to the right. Rule 14, statement-3, is either a sentence or a tu'e ... tu'u block. The block makes a whole text-1 act as a single sentence, both for connection and for a tense placed before it. Its tu'u is elidable, and carries its own free-modifier slot.

A prenex can stand only at the start of a statement. After .i with a connective, and after .i bo, the rules allow no separate prenex, though a tu'e ... tu'u block can hold one. A fragment can stand beside a bare .i only. The third baseline removed fragments as operands of sentence connectives on purpose, so .i je joins statements and nothing smaller.
An utterance that is not a sentence is a fragment, under rule 20 (see and ). A fragment is one of these:

listitem.para: A bare connective, as the answer to a ji or gi'i question.
A bare quantifier, as the answer to xo.
A list of terms, with an optional vau.
A be or bei phrase that supplies arguments after the fact.

section.para: Since a list of terms is a fragment, le sutra tavla fits the rules in two ways. It is a fragment, the single description the fast talker. It is also a sentence, the fast one talks, with ku elided. explains how this grammar chooses between the two.

listitem.para: ek # | gihek # | quantifier | NA # | terms /VAU#/ | prenex | relative-clauses | links | linkargs

section.title: Sentences and bridi-tails
section.para: A sentence, rule 40, is a bridi: some terms, then optionally cu, then the bridi-tail, which holds the selbri and any terms that follow it (see ). The terms before the selbri are called the head, and cu marks where the head ends. It lets a description close without its ku, since cu cannot continue the selbri of the description. The terms are optional, so a sentence may begin with its selbri, as klama alone does.
A subsentence, rule 41, is either a sentence or a prenex followed by a subsentence. Abstractions and relative clauses contain subsentences, and the prenex of a subsentence is local to it (see ).

The bridi-tail rules state how sentences come to share a head under a gihek, the connective family of gi'e, gi'a and the rest of GIhA (see ). Rule 53, bridi-tail-3, is a single selbri with its tail terms, or else a forethought gek-sentence. Rule 52 binds two tails with gihek [stag] bo, and groups to the right. Rule 51 joins tails with a plain gihek, and groups to the left (see ). Each tail after a gihek has its own tail terms. Four tails, for instance, group as ((A gi'e B) gi'a C) gi'u D.

Rule 50, bridi-tail, lets a gihek be followed by ke ... ke'e, with an optional tense or modal on the connective before the ke. The brackets group the tails inside them against the tail to the left. The tail terms after the whole connection apply to both sides of it, just as they do after a plain gihek (see ). So in mi broda gi'e ke brode ke'e le zarci, le zarci applies to broda and to the group alike. The tail terms after each selbri belong to that selbri, and vau closes them; it is almost always elided.

After a gihek, ke can begin either a group of tails or a tanru unit of the next tail. Where both readings fit the text, this grammar takes the group (see ). A tense between the gihek and the ke then belongs to the connective. In mi klama gi'e pu ke cadzu ke'e, pu sits on the connective, as teaches. Where only the plain reading fits, it stands: in mi broda gi'e ke brode ke'e brodi, the tail goes on after ke'e, so the group cannot read it. also contrasts written and elided ke'e when vau follows.

A gek-sentence, rule 54, joins two subsentences in forethought (see ). Forethought introduces a connection before its first operand, and the gek itself can contain a tense, as in pu gi A gi B. The tail terms after the whole connection apply to both sides. A gek-sentence can also stand inside ke ... ke'e, with a tense or modal before the ke, or after na.

EBNF grammarcorrections, gek-sentenceRule 54 is corrected here. The first edition printed the tense or modal before ke as optional, but both versions of that rule in the YACC grammar require it, and nothing in this book uses the bare form. This edition prints tag KE. The example in , mi bai ke ge klama le zarci gi cadzu le bisli, has its tag.

A bare tense can stand before a forethought connection, as in mi pu ge klama le zarci gi tervecnu lo cidja (see ). That text fits these rules with pu as a term and its ku elided, so the tense has scope over the whole connection. says why the elided ku is allowed there. The official parser, however, requires the written pu ku, and so would any reader who wants to see at once that the tense covers both connected bridi.

listitem.para: gek subsentence gik subsentence tail-terms | tag KE # gek-sentence /KEhE#/ | NA # gek-sentence

section.title: Terms
section.para: A term, rule 83, is one argument of a bridi, or else one tense or modal standing on its own (see , and ). It is any one of these:

listitem.para: A sumti, or ku written or elided, after a tense, a modal or a place marker fa, fe, and the rest: ca lo nu broda, fi mi, pu ku.
A termset after a tense or modal.
na ku, the sentence-level negation written as a term.

section.para: A tense or modal with nothing after it takes ku, so that it won't swallow the next sumti. When what follows cannot be a sumti, the ku may be elided. When what follows can be a sumti, says which reading wins. A tense or modal placed directly before a selbri binds to that selbri, as teaches, and that same subsection states the rule.

The three levels of terms state the termset connectives (see and ). A termset is simply a set of terms. Rule 82 joins terms into a termset with ce'e, as in mi ce'e do. Rule 81 joins termsets with pe'e followed by a jek or a joik, the afterthought form that connects two sets of arguments at once. Those connections group from the left, as afterthought logical connectives do; the ce'e of a termset, however, groups nothing. A termset in forethought is nu'i gek terms nu'u gik terms nu'u. And nu'i terms nu'u by itself brackets several terms into one, so that a connective applies to all of them.
A tense or modal before a termset governs the whole termset, as in zu'a nu'i la .djordj. la'u lo mitre be li mu nu'u (see ). If a ku is written, it ends the tag as a separate term.

termsetswith a preceding tag, in the EBNF grammarThe form tag termset in rule 83 is an addition of this edition. The third baseline has no such form, either in the EBNF or in the YACC grammar; its parser reads the tag and the termset as two separate terms. teaches the structure with the tag over the termset, and its examples show it. The errata of the first edition recorded the conflict but offered no fix. This edition follows the text of the book.

listitem.para: sumti | (tag | FA #) (sumti | /KU#/) | termset | tag termset | NA KU #
NUhI # gek terms /NUhU#/ gik terms /NUhU#/ | NUhI # terms /NUhU#/

section.title: Sumti
section.para: A sumti is an argument: a description, a name, a pronoun, a quotation, a number, or a connection of these (see ). The levels from sumti down to sumti-4 state the connectives and their grouping, in the same shape as for statements and bridi-tails.

Rule 91 is a sumti with a ke ... ke'e grouped connection after it. Rule 92 is a sequence joined in afterthought by an ek or a joik, as in mi .e do or mi joi do, and it groups from the left (see ). Rule 93 is the bo form, which groups from the right (see ). Rule 94 is either a simple sumti or a forethought connection, ge mi gi do. The top rule adds vu'o followed by relative clauses, which attach to the whole connected sumti rather than to its last member (see ).

Rule 95 places the outer quantifier. A number before a simple sumti counts its referents, as in re lo gerku. A quantifier directly before a selbri also makes a sumti, re gerku, and the ku of that form is elidable. explains it as re da poi gerku, which is not the same as re lo gerku. Relative clauses can follow either one.

Rule 97, sumti-6, is the closed list of simple sumti. A LAhE word such as la'e, or a NAhE word with bo such as na'e bo, qualifies another sumti, and lu'u closes the result. KOhA is a pronoun. A lerfu string such as .abu or xy. is a sumti, and boi closes it and separates it from a following number or lerfu string. la before cmevla makes a name, and a relative clause can stand between la and the name words, as in la poi melbi ku'o .alis., Alice the Beautiful (see ). la or le, that is, any member of LA or LE, before a sumti-tail makes a description closed by ku. li opens a mekso, a mathematical expression, closed by lo'o. Four forms quote (see and ):

listitem.para: zo quotes the single next word.
lu ... li'u quotes a Lojban text.
lo'u ... le'u quotes a run of Lojban words that need not be grammatical, possibly none.
zoi quotes any text between two copies of a delimiter word.

section.para: The word-level rules of delimit each zo, lo'u and zoi quote before the grammar ever sees the text (see ), and the any-word and anything in rule 97 are a picture of that work. A lu ... li'u quote is different: it holds a whole text, which the grammar reads with the rules of this section. Its free-modifier slot follows the quote whether or not li'u is written.

EBNF grammarcorrections, sumti-6Rule 97 is corrected in two places. First, the first edition printed LOhU any-word ... LEhU, which requires at least one word between the delimiters. The YACC grammar reads the quoted words as one unit that can be empty, so lo'u le'u is a sumti. Second, the first edition printed LU text /LIhU#/, which drops the free-modifier slot together with an elided li'u. The YACC grammar attaches free modifiers to the whole quote, so lu cy. to toi is a quote followed by a parenthesis. This edition prints LU text /LIhU/ #.

Rule 111, sumti-tail, is what follows a descriptor (see ). It begins with an optional inner sumti that possesses or restricts, as in le mi zdani (see ). Then come the inner quantifier and the selbri, le ci gerku, or else a quantifier and a sumti, lo re lo gerku. Relative clauses can come after the inner sumti, and they can also replace it (see ).

section.title: Relative clauses
section.para: A relative clause attaches to a sumti and either restricts it or comments on it (see ). goi and the other members of GOI take a term, as in mi goi ko'a or le zdani pe mi, and ge'u closes the clause. poi, noi and voi take a subsentence in which ke'a refers back to the sumti, and ku'o closes the clause. zi'e joins several relative clauses on one sumti, and it groups nothing (see ).

section.title: Selbri and tanru
section.para: A selbri is the predicate of a bridi (see ), and a tense or modal can come before it. When a tense or modal is not written as a term, that is how it attaches to the whole bridi, as in mi pu klama. The levels below state the tanru grouping. Rule 131 allows na before a selbri, which is the contradictory negation (see ).

Rule 132 is the co inversion, sutra co tavla. It swaps the order of modifier and modified, so that the part after co is the modifier (see ). The whole selbri keeps the place structure of the part before co, and co groups to the right.
Rule 133 is a plain tanru: a sequence of units with no connective between them. It groups to the left, by the left-grouping rule of tanru (see ), so barda gerku zdani is (barda gerku) zdani.

Rule 134 joins units by a jek or a joik in afterthought, as in barda je melbi, or by a joik followed by ke ... ke'e, with an optional tense or modal on the connective. These connections group from the left (see ). A joik directly before ke can often be read in two ways: as the ke group, or as a plain connection to a unit that happens to begin with ke. Where both fit the text, this grammar takes the group (see ). A jek has no such form, so mi broda je ke brode ke'e is a plain connection.

Rule 135 joins units by a jek or a joik with bo, as in melbi je bo cmalu nixli. Such a connection binds more tightly than plain juxtaposition, and a run of bo groups from the right (see ). Rule 136 is a tanru unit, optionally followed by bo and a further unit of the same rule, as in melbi cmalu bo nixli. A run of tanru bo groups from the right too, so cmalu bo nixli bo ckule (see ) is cmalu bo (nixli bo ckule). Rule 136 can also be a forethought connection with a guhek, as in gu'e barda gi melbi, optionally negated by na'e (see ).

A tanru unit is one brick of the selbri. Rule 150 joins units with cei to assign an antecedent to a pro-bridi, a predicate pronoun such as broda: klama cei broda. This grammatical position does not restrict the antecedent to one unit. The pro-bridi can stand for a whole selbri or even a whole bridi, as explains. Rule 151 attaches linked arguments, be ... bei ... be'o, which fill the places of that one unit and not those of the whole bridi (see ). Rule 152 lists the simple units:

listitem.para: A pro-bridi of GOhA, with optional ra'o.
me sumti me'u, which turns a sumti into a selbri, optionally with a following MOI word.
A number or lerfu string with moi, mei or another word of MOI.
A conversion: se, te, ve or xe.
jai with an optional tense or modal.
A zei compound, which the word-level rules of have already made into one brivla (see ).

An abstraction: nu, ka, du'u or another word of NU before a subsentence, closed by kei. A jek or a joik can connect several abstraction words, as in nu je ka, and the connection groups from the left (see ).

section.para: The SE, JAI and NAhE forms refer back to rule 152 itself, so se se broda and na'e se broda are single units.

EBNF grammarcorrections, tanru-unit-2Rule 152 is corrected in one place. The first edition printed the zei compound without a free-modifier slot, although every other unit has one. The YACC grammar merges a compound into one brivla before parsing, and then allows a free modifier after it, as after any brivla. So mi broda zei brode to do toi is a sentence, and this edition prints the slot.

section.title: Numbers, lerfu strings and mekso
section.para: A number, rule 812, is a string of PA words, such as the digits pa and re and the decimal point pi (see ). Either PA words or lerfu words may follow its first word: pa re ci, pa xy.. A lerfu string, rule 817, starts with a lerfu word instead (see ). A lerfu word, rule 987, is a BY word, a lau shift before a lerfu word, or a tei ... foi compound (see and ). The word-level rules of turn each word with bu into a single BY word before the grammar ever sees it, and the any-word BU of rule 987 is a picture of that (see ).

A number or lerfu string cannot end before another number word or lerfu word. A written boi is what ends the run. So pa xy. cu barda is not a sentence, and pa boi xy. cu barda is one (see and ). This holds even where dividing the run is the only way to make the rest of the text fit. The notation has no way of writing that rule, so it is stated here, and lists it among the rules on which readings count.

A quantifier, rule 300, is a number closed by boi, or a mekso in vei ... ve'o brackets (see ). Rule 310 permits afterthought infix expressions, such as li pa su'i re, and reverse Polish expressions introduced by fu'a. In reverse Polish notation, an expression is two operands followed by an operator, and each operand can itself be such an expression (see ). Infix operators group to the left, so ci su'i vo pi'i mu is (ci su'i vo) pi'i mu (see ). Rule 311 is the bi'e form, which binds an operator more tightly than its neighbors; a run of bi'e groups from the right. Rule 312 is an operand, or a forethought operator followed by its operands. An optional pe'o comes before the operator, and an optional ku'e after the last operand.

Operators have their own connectives and grouping, shaped just like those of selbri (see ). Rule 370 joins operators by a jek or a joik, or by a joik and a ke group, and these connections group from the left. Where a joik stands directly before ke, this grammar takes the group where both readings fit (see ). Rule 371 supplies the guhek forethought and the bo forms. Rule 372 is a simple operator or a ke ... ke'e group. A simple operator, rule 374, is a VUhU word, possibly converted by se or negated by na'e. It can also be an operator made from a mekso through ma'o, or a selbri used as an operator through na'u; te'u closes these last two.

Operands connect in the same way. Rule 381 takes a ke group, rule 382 the afterthought connectives, and rule 383 the bo form, with the same grouping as for sumti. Rule 385 lists the simple operands: a quantifier, a lerfu string, a selbri through ni'e, a sumti through mo'e, and an array through jo'i. A forethought connection counts as a simple operand too, and so does a qualifier such as la'e or na'e bo before an operand.

section.title: Logical and non-logical connectives
section.para: Lojban has just one set of logical connectives, though it spells them differently at each level of the grammar (see ). An ek joins sumti, as in .e and .a. A gihek joins bridi-tails, as in gi'e. A jek joins tanru units and, when preceded by .i, sentences, as in je. A gek is the forethought form, ga ... gi. Every afterthought logical connective can be negated on either side, with na before it and nai after it, and can be converted by se.

A joik is a non-logical connective: joi, ce, jo'u and the rest of JOI, or else an interval connective, bi'i or bi'o. An interval has ga'o or ke'i on both sides or on neither (see and ). A joik can have se before it and nai after it, but no corresponding initial na. Rules 421 and 422, joik-ek and joik-jek, are the pairs that stand in the same position, each with a slot for a free modifier.

A gek, rule 807, is a forethought logical connective. It can also be a joik used in forethought with gi, or a tense with gi, as in pu gi ... gi. A gik, rule 816, separates the two halves, and is just gi, optionally negated. A guhek, rule 808, is the forethought connective for tanru units and for operators.

keafter a connective, in the EBNF grammarSeveral rules let a connective take a ke ... ke'e group: rule 50 for a gihek, rules 91 and 381 for an ek or a joik, and rules 134 and 370 for a joik. In each of them an optional tense or modal may stand between the connective and the ke, and it belongs to the connective (see ). has .e pu ke, and has gi'e ca ke. For bridi-tails, tanru units, and operators, the same words can also fit a plain connection to a unit that happens to begin with ke. Where both readings fit the whole text, this grammar takes the group. A simple sumti or mathematical operand cannot begin with ke, so those levels have no competing plain reading. A free modifier that is still a word of its own, such as a parenthesis, breaks the pattern: mi broda gi'e to do toi ke brode ke'e has a plain gi'e. Where only the plain reading fits, the plain reading stands, so these three are all sentences: mi broda joi ke brode ke'e bo brodi, mi broda gi'e ke brode ke'e brodi and mi broda gi'e ke brode ke'e vau do.

The official parser reads a connective directly before ke as one unit before it applies the rules, and so it rejects the three sentences above. This grammar follows the printed rules, which accept them. Where both readings fit, the two agree.

Written vau by itself does not settle the choice. In mi broda gi'e ke brode vau do, ke'e is elided before do, and vau closes the tail terms inside the group. The do follows the group and applies to both tails. Compare the last sentence above, mi broda gi'e ke brode ke'e vau do. Here the written ke'e closes a tanru unit, and vau closes that tail's terms. The do follows the whole connection, so only the plain reading fits.

section.title: Tenses and modals
section.para: A tense or modal, rule 491 tag, turns a sumti into a modal or tense term (see and ), and it can also mark a selbri or a whole sentence with a tense. A tag is one or more tense-modals joined by a jek or a joik, as in pu je ca, and such connections group from the left (see and ). Rule 971, stag, is the restricted form that is allowed inside connectives before bo and ke, and in a gek. It has no free-modifier slot, because a slot there would make the grammar ambiguous.

A tense-modal, rule 815, is either a simple tense-modal with a free-modifier slot, or fi'o selbri fe'u, which makes a modal out of any selbri (see ). A simple tense-modal, rule 972, has one of these forms:

listitem.para: A BAI modal, optionally converted by se.
A time tense, a space tense, or both in either order, followed by an optional CAhA word such as ka'e. A CAhA word can also stand alone.

section.para: na'e can negate either a BAI modal or a tense, and ki can follow either one. So ba za ki, na'e ka'e and pu ki are each a single simple tense-modal.

EBNF grammarcorrections, simple-tense-modalRule 972 is corrected here. The first edition printed its second alternative as [NAhE] (time [space] | space [time]) & CAhA [KI]. Under the precedence of point 11 of the notation, that attaches na'e to the tense alone and ki to the CAhA word alone. The YACC grammar puts both around the whole combination, and this edition adds the parentheses that say so.

A time tense, rule 1030, contains these parts in this order (see and ): a zi distance, offsets pu, ca, ba each with an optional distance, an interval ze'a with an optional direction, and interval properties. A space tense, rule 1040, is likewise built from a va distance, offsets of FAhA, a space interval, and a mo'i movement. A space interval is ve'a or vi'a or both, with an optional direction, and then interval properties, each flagged by fe'e (see ). An interval property, rule 1051, is roi with a number, a word of TAhE such as ta'e, or a ZAhO event contour, and each of these can take nai. A tense can hold a whole string of them, as in (see ).

Time usually comes before space, as advises, but the rule allows both orders, so mi va pu klama has the one tense va pu. Sometimes the words of a tense can be divided in more than one way. When that happens, this grammar takes the earliest tense, and then the longest. A longer tense counts only where a reading of the whole text remains with it (see ). That matters before gi. In mi viska pu ca gi do gi la .djan. the connective is pu ca gi. In mi viska pu va ca gi do gi la .djan., though, two divisions begin at pu: the tense pu va and then the connective ca gi, or the tense pu and then the connective va ca gi. pu va is the longer tense, so the first division wins. (pu va ca is not one tense, because a tense does not return to time after its space part.)

The limit on the longest tense is this edition's. A longer tense is taken only where a reading of the whole text remains with it. The lexer of the official grammar forms the longest tense in every case, even where no reading remains. No known text shows the difference.

section.title: Free modifiers, vocatives and indicators
section.para: A free modifier, rule 32, can occupy any # slot, and permits free modifiers after many constructions. The forms are these:

listitem.para: A sei ... se'u discursive bridi, sei mi cusku.
A vocative phrase: coi or doi and their kin, alone or followed by a selbri, by names, or by a sumti. Relative clauses can surround the selbri or the names, and the whole phrase is closed by do'u.
A subscript xi with a number, a lerfu string or a bracketed mekso.

section.para: The se'u, do'u, toi, boi and ve'o of rule 32 are all elidable, but the rule writes them without #. The slot that follows a free modifier is the one that the modifier itself sits in. So a subscript after a lerfu string needs a written boi to attach to: xy. boi xi ky.. The rules do not accept xy. xi ky., even though prints exactly that form. That example is one of the known conflicts between the first edition's examples and its own grammar, and this chapter does not resolve it.

A vocative, rule 415, is a run of COI words, each with an optional nai, or else doi, or both in that order. Indicators, rule 411, are a run of indicator words, optionally opened by fu'e. An indicator word is an attitudinal or discursive of UI or CAI with an optional nai, or the cancel da'o, or fu'o. The fu'o closes a scope that fu'e opened (see ).

The grammar reads indicators as separate words only at the start of a text. Everywhere else the word-level rules attach them to the word before them, so the rules of this section never see them (see ).

Rule 413 lists Y, the hesitation sound .y., among the indicators. Under the rules of , ordinary hesitation is invisible to the grammar, so this alternative never applies. It stays in the rule because that is how the first edition printed it.

section.title: From words to the grammar
section.para: EBNF grammarinput ofThe rules of this section read a stream of words, each of which carries a class. explains how a text is divided into words. Every cmavo belongs to a selma'o, and lists them all; every gismu, lujvo and fu'ivla has the class BRIVLA, and every name word has the class CMEVLA. The word-form grammar adds three things that the lists of the first edition lacked: a digit is a PA word, .ybu is a BY word, and a run of .y. counts as one hesitation.

Between the word forms and the grammar stand the magic words: the quotations, zei, bu, the erasers si, sa and su, hesitation, and fa'o. specifies them, rule by rule and with the status of each. They do their work before the grammar ever sees the text. (The parser of the first edition prepared the words in its own older sequence of steps, which the YACC supplement gives.)

Some rules of this section mention ZEI, BU, SI, SA and SU. These rules picture work that the magic words have already done. The grammar proper sees a single BRIVLA for a zei compound and a single BY for a word with bu, and an eraser and whatever it erased never reach the grammar at all. A reader applies each of these once, at the word level, and the rules then see every compound as one word.
indicatorsattachment, in the EBNF grammarIndicators and ba'e attach to words before the grammar reads them, by the rules of and :

listitem.para: Indicators at the start of a text stay in the stream. They modify everything that follows, and rule 0 reads them.
A quoted text starts just as a whole text does, so indicators right after lu begin the quoted text. The parser of the first edition attached them to lu instead, which its author called an error.
Indicators right after tu'e attach to tu'e, because its rule reads text-1, and that has no place for indicators at its start.
Indicators right after to and to'i attach to the opener and mark the whole parenthetical remark, as shows with to'i sa'a.

Every other run of indicators attaches to the word before it, including a name and a closing word such as li'u or toi. After a completed zo, lo'u ... le'u or zoi quotation, the indicators comment on the whole quotation, as says.
ba'e marks the word after it, so ba'e zo coi marks zo.
A nai joins a UI or CAI word directly before it; any other nai stays a word for the grammar. So in mi .e ui da'o nai do klama, the ui and da'o attach to .e, and the nai negates the .e.

section.para: The rule for to and to'i is a choice of this edition. Rule 32 reads a parenthesis as TO text, and a text can begin with indicators, so the rules alone would treat to just as they treat lu. But a parenthetical remark does not begin the way a quoted text does. puts the indicator on the opener, and so does the committee's definition of to'i as to sa'a.
Ordinary hesitation, .y., does not reach the grammar (see ). The Y of rule 413 is a historical alternative, as says.

Three rules that the notation cannot write also belong to the reading of a text. A number or lerfu string cannot be divided before another number word or lerfu word (see ). Where both readings fit, a connective, an optional tense or modal, and ke form the ke group. The words of a tense are divided at the earliest and then the longest tense. states the last two.
The following rules are non-formal. They describe the stream of words rather than its grammar:

para.quote: any text at all, whether Lojban or not

listitem.para: any-word SI | utterance SA | text SU

section.para: Rule 1100 says what a word is, for the purposes of the rules above: an optional run of emphasis words, the word itself, and any indicators attached to it. The whole run of ba'e words goes with the next word that is not itself ba'e, and a ba'e at the end of a text is an error. For an eraser, however, still counts each ba'e as a word of its own: broda ba'e da si da erases only the da.

EBNF grammarcorrections, wordRule 1100 is corrected. The first edition printed [BAhE], which allows one emphasis word at most. The YACC grammar absorbs every ba'e into the word after it, so several can stand before a single word. This edition prints [BAhE ...].

any-word is any single word, and anything is any text at all, Lojban or not. Rule 1101, null, pictures the erasers: si erases the word before it, sa erases back to the start of an utterance, and su erases a whole text. gives their rules and the status of each. (The first edition never defined the utterance that sa erases, by the way.)
FAhO is a universal terminator and signals the end of parsable input.

section.title: Choosing among readings
section.para: elidable terminatorschoosing among readings, in the EBNF grammarPoint 10 of the notation allows an elidable terminator to be omitted wherever no grammatical ambiguity results, but it never says how to decide that none does. As the rules stand, several texts are left with more than one reading, a reading being one way in which the words of a whole text can be made to fit the rules. This subsection gives the rules by which this grammar chooses a single reading, so that every text has at most one structure.

elidable terminatorsrule of this editionThe rule for elided terminators is this edition's own; point 10 of the notation does not require it. It is one way of keeping the promise of point 10, and it proceeds in the steps below.

listitem.para: A terminator can be elided wherever a reading of the whole text needs it.
Where a text has several readings, the four rules of the list that follows this one are applied first.

For each reading that remains, count the terminators it elides at each position, working from the start of the text. At the first position where the counts differ, the reading with fewer elided terminators there wins. Two readings with the same counts at every position are tied, whatever the terminators happen to be called, and a tie is an error.

Whenever the chosen reading elides a terminator, write the elided terminators of that reading back into the text, and read the text again. This holds whether the count chose the reading among several or it was the only reading from the start. In this second reading every elidable place holds either a written or a restored terminator, and several terminators restored at one place keep their order.

The second reading applies the four rules again, but it judges them by the original words and not by the restored terminators, since a restored terminator is not a word the speaker wrote. So a restored ku does not count as the written ku that keeps a tag a term. The count, however, is not applied a second time.

A restored terminator can stand where the words after it cannot complete the rest of its construct. One with nothing after it inside its construct makes one reading, not two. A restored /X#/ restores X alone, with no free modifier. Another reading can still take a restored terminator as an ordinary word and start a longer construct there.

The second reading must still find the chosen reading, and it must find no other. If the four rules now reject the chosen reading, the text is an error. If two readings remain, the text is also an error, because its ambiguity is not about terminators. A reading that elides no terminator needs no second reading.

section.para: The second reading keeps the rules of the list below in force. mi viska pu ca gi do gi la .djan. vau, with its vau written, still has two divisions of pu ca gi, and the tense rule still chooses the connective pu ca gi.
These four rules apply before the count, and in this order:

listitem.para: A number or lerfu string cannot be divided before another number word or lerfu word (see ). A reading that divides such a run is not a reading at all.

Where the words of a tense can be divided in more than one way, the earliest tense is taken, and then the longest (see ). A longer tense counts only where a reading remains. This fixes the span of each tense before the next rule looks at it.

A tense or modal that stands directly before a selbri, with no ku between them, binds to that selbri. A reading that makes such a tag a term with its ku elided is not a reading. A written ku keeps the tag a term. A tense or modal inside a connective, as in gi'e pu ke, is not a term, so this rule says nothing about it.

A connective, an optional tense or modal, and ke stand together. Where both the ke group and a plain connection fit the text, the group is taken, and the tense or modal then belongs to the connective (see ).

section.para: tagsbinding to selbri, in the EBNF grammarThe third rule is the decision on tag binding of the BPFK, the language-definition committee. Seven of its eight members approved it on 15 March 2016, and the LLG never separately ratified it. The decision reads: a tense or tag attaches tightly to a following selbri unless explicitly terminated by ku. So lo nu broda ba brode is a complete bridi, whose abstraction closes before ba (see and ). Without this rule, the count alone would keep ba inside the abstraction, as the grammar of the first edition did. The rule is a requirement, not a preference: lo nu broda ba brode cu brodi is an error, because ba must bind to brode and then nothing can take cu brodi, whereas lo nu broda ba ku brode cu brodi is a sentence. In lo nu broda va pu brode, the second rule makes va pu one tense, and the whole of it belongs to brode. A tag followed by a sumti, as in lo nu klama ba le nu tavla cu xamgu, stays a term inside the abstraction.
Here are some texts and their readings under these rules:

listitem.para: le sutra tavla is a fragment, the one description the fast talker. The sentence reading would elide a ku after sutra, while the fragment reading elides its ku only at the end. A speaker who means the sentence says le sutra cu tavla.
le lojbo se farvi le loglo gi'enai mintu ja dunli le logla is a sentence. The description le lojbo ends before se farvi, because no other reading fits the whole text.
le nanmu joi le ninmu cu klama is a sentence with two connected sumti, since no reading of the whole text keeps joi inside the description.
mi pu ge klama le zarci gi tervecnu lo cidja is a sentence, with pu a term and its ku elided before the forethought connection.

section.para: elidable terminatorsthe official parser andThe official parser applies point 10 differently. It reads one unit ahead and never goes back, a unit being a word, or a run of words that the parser has already joined. A tense is one unit, and so is a connective together with its ke. The parser therefore elides a terminator only where the next unit cannot continue what it is reading, and so it rejects some texts that this grammar accepts. Two of them are le nanmu joi le ninmu cu klama and the bare tense before a forethought connection. Several passages of the first edition described that behavior as a rule of the language, and this edition corrects them where they occur. In each of these cases the written terminator remains the clear way to write the text. Without it, a reader cannot easily see where a construct ends: where one selbri ends and the next begins, or that one tense covers both connected bridi.

section.title: Changes from the third baseline
section.para: EBNF grammarchanges from the third baselineThis grammar departs from the EBNF of the third baseline in the places listed here, and each departure is marked at the spot where it is made. lists them again among the changes from the first edition.
First come the corrections: places where the first edition's EBNF misprinted what the grammar meant, and where the YACC grammar shows the intended form (all editorial):

listitem.para: Rule 2: a text can begin with .i forms and then ni'o markers ().
Rule 54: a gek-sentence wrapped in ke requires the tense or modal before the ke ().
Rule 97: lo'u le'u can be empty, and the free-modifier slot after lu ... li'u follows the whole quote ().
Rule 152: a zei compound has a free-modifier slot ().
Rule 972: na'e and ki cover the whole tense ().
Rule 1100: several ba'e can stand before a single word ().

section.para: The notation itself gains points 11 to 13 and the restriction in point 6 (editorial, ). They change no rule.
Next, the changes that the text of this book requires:

listitem.para: Rule 83: a tense or modal before a termset governs the whole termset (editorial, ).
A tense or modal placed directly before a selbri binds to that selbri (committee-approved in 2016, ).

section.para: Then come the departures from the official parser, which follow from this edition's reading of the rules (all editorial):

listitem.para: The rule for elided terminators, and the choice among readings ().
Texts that fit only the plain reading of a connective before ke are grammatical ().
A bare tense before a forethought connection is grammatical ().

When a tense is divided, the division takes a longer tense only where a reading remains, whereas the lexer of the official grammar forms the longest tense in every case; no known text shows the difference ().

section.para: Two further choices of this edition carry their marks where they are made. Indicators after to and to'i attach to the opener (editorial, ), and the Y of rule 413 stays as a historical alternative ().
